transcript:
Meeting header:
2026-03-16 14:00 PDT | Duration: 1:15 | Attendees: Elena Martinez (Redwood AE), Derek Shaw (Redwood SE), Nina Park (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Summit Head of Eng), Marcus Li (Platform), Dana Owens (Security), Omar Reed (Data Scientist)

[00:00] Elena: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Elena from Redwood, I'll hand over to Derek to kick off with a quick agenda.
[00:12] Derek: Hey all — quick agenda: one, get a sense for current infra and workloads; two, define POC success criteria; three, workload sizing and benchmarks; four, timeline and next steps.
[00:24] Priya: Sounds good. To give context — Summit Payments is building a real-time transaction risk scoring API that enriches transaction metadata and returns a short explanation and score. We currently do ~150 RPS peak across us-east and eu-west with a 99th percentile latency target of 250ms for the whole service. Model stage today is a fine-tuned 7B open model hosted on k8s (mix of CPU + a few GPUs).
[00:48] Marcus: To add — typical request token size is about 120 tokens in, 40 tokens out. Average latency from app -> model is about 200ms but bursty during peak.
[01:05] Derek: Great, that gives us a good baseline. Quick question: is the 150 RPS evenly distributed or spiky?
[01:12] Priya: Spiky — we see sustained 60-80 RPS and spikes up to 180 for short periods. Also we need multi-region support, eu data residency for some accounts.
[01:23] Nina: On compliance, do you need customer-managed keys or is cloud KMS ok?
[01:29] Dana: We prefer customer KMS for production, but for the POC cloud KMS is fine as long as logs are auditable. Also need SOC2 and ISO docs.
[01:40] Derek: Noted. Now success criteria — what would make the POC a win for you?
[01:45] Priya: Three things: (1) P95 latency under 300ms end-to-end for the LLM portion, (2) cost per 1M tokens that is competitive — we have an internal target, and (3) minimal integration effort and compatibility with our VPC and SSO.
[01:58] Marcus: Also, we want reproducible benchmark results and a path to scale to dedicated capacity if needed.
[02:05] Elena: Understood. Quick framing on deployment modes: hosted = fastest to spin up, lower engineering lift, Redwood manages infra; dedicated = reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and better tail latency and data isolation; private = customer-controlled VPC/on-prem for strict compliance. There are tradeoffs across latency, cost, and operational control.
[02:29] Derek: For workload sizing, based on ~150 RPS and 160 tokens total per request, rough token throughput estimate is 150 * 160 * 60 = ~1.44M tokens/min at sustained peak — though spikes increase concurrency demands. We'll need to look at concurrency not just RPS, since KV cache and batching behavior change efficiency.
[02:52] Omar: Wait that calc — tokens per minute seems high, can you run that again?
[02:56] Derek: Sure. 150 requests/sec * 160 tokens = 24,000 tokens/sec = 1.44M tokens/min. If your average is lower during most of the day, we can dimension the POC to mimic both steady and spike profiles.
[03:12] Priya: For the POC we can provide a 24-hour traffic sample reflecting spikes.
[03:18] Derek: Excellent, that'll help. For benchmarking plan: week 0 — onboarding and infra setup (hosted fastest, dedicated takes 1–2 days to reserve nodes, private depends on customer's network approvals); week 1 — baseline hosted tests; week 2 — dedicated config and tests; week 3 — private (if pursuing) or soak tests; week 4 — analysis and handoff.
[03:40] Marcus: If we do dedicated, what's the lead time for reserved capacity?
[03:44] Elena: Reserved pools can be provisioned in 48–72 hours once sizing is agreed, but private VPC network setup can take longer depending on your networking team.
[03:52] Dana: About security: how do you handle KV cache and logs? Are logs stored in Redwood or forwarded?
[03:59] Nina: By default logs are in the customer's account for private deployments, for hosted we provide audit logs and can forward to your SIEM. KV cache contents are ephemeral and not persisted to customer logs. We'll share an architecture diagram.
[04:14] Priya: Latency concern — our end-to-end P95 target includes network hop, so we need Redwood token latency to be comfortably below 200ms.
[04:22] Derek: Operationally we typically see per-token latency numbers for a 7–13B model in hosted mode that meet your target for small sequences when batched effectively; dedicated with pinned GPUs gets better tail latency. We'll include P50/P95/P99 metrics in the benchmark report.
[04:36] Elena: Cost — you'll want cost per 1M tokens and cost per concurrent request. Hosted mode typically has higher per-token but lower operational overhead; dedicated reduces unit cost at higher commit levels. We can model your traffic to show cost curves.
[04:50] Omar: Any model quantization or mixed-precision recommendations? It affects latency and quality.
[04:54] Derek: Yes — we'll recommend quantization profiles for your model family. For a 7B fine-tuned model, int8/4 quantization is common; Redwood Optimize will suggest profiles based on your eval prompts. We'll include a quality regression check in the POC so we don't degrade outputs.
[05:10] Priya: On quality: we need to preserve certain deterministic behaviors — must not hallucinate regulatory flags. Can you run our eval suite?
[05:16] Nina: Absolutely — please send a prompt set and expected outputs. We'll tie evals to benchmark runs and report regressions.
[05:24] Marcus: For networking, will hosted require opening inbound rules or is outbound-only sufficient?
[05:29] Derek: Hosted uses outbound to Redwood endpoints; dedicated and private can be VPC peering or private link. We'll document firewall requirements.
[05:38] Dana: For PII, any token-level retention policies?
[05:41] Elena: We support configurable retention; for private deployments you control storage. For hosted we have options for non-retention for POC contexts and entitlements for production.
[05:50] Priya: Ok timeline — we want to start next week and have a go/no-go decision by mid-April. Is that feasible?
[05:56] Derek: Yes — a 4-week POC starting 2026-03-22 fits that timeline. Week 1: hosted baseline + evals; week 2: dedicated + adjustments; week 3: soak and regression checks; week 4: results and runbook for production.
[06:10] Elena: Recap of next steps: Elena will send pricing and SLA matrix; Derek will share benchmark plan and scripts; Priya will send traffic sample and eval prompts; Dana will collect compliance questions.
[06:21] Priya: Sounds good. One more thing — network egress costs, especially for eu-west routing, can change our cost calculus. Can you show region-aware cost estimates?
[06:29] Elena: Yes we'll include region cost breakdowns in the pricing sheet.
[06:33] Marcus: For the POC, can we run a 1-hour high-concurrency spike test to validate tail latency?
[06:37] Derek: Yes — we'll schedule controlled spike tests during week 2.
[06:40] Omar: Also please include model-version pinning and rollback procedure in the runbook.
[06:45] Nina: We'll include rollout options: canary, A/B, auto-fallback to smaller model if latency breaches.
[06:51] Priya: Great. That covers all my questions.
[06:54] Elena: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and calendar invites.
[07:00] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker attributions may be approximate, occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., KV / k V cache noted as K V cache).
